messages.author: 5fb191f8527859e2
messages.subject: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
parts:
Dear all,
 
I would like to use the Dail-Madsen model to analyse data collected by volunteers. It is data where volunteers captured toads and carried them across roads to prevent mortality of toads on the roads. The main question is to test for a trend in abundance (in the unmarked language it would be pcountOpen(… , dynamics=”trend”, …)) . JAGS code for such a model is available in the electronic supplement of the paper by Hostetler and Chandler.
 
We have data from 153 sites and a period of 30 years (1985 to 2014). However, average length of the time series is only about 9 years. Site-speficif data are for different time periods. That is, for one site we may have data from, say, 1985 to 1995, for another site the data may be from 2000 to 2010. Data for a third site data may be from 1997 to 2002.
 
The Dail-Madsen model estimates an initial abundance, N[i,1] (where i stands for site i). In my data set this would be N[i,1984]. I think it makes no sense to estimate this abundance because for most sites there is simply no data for the first year (1984) of the data set. Because it is a kind of a “staggered entry” design, I think it would be preferable to estimate a site-specific first year abundance.
 
Would it be possible to replace N[i,1] with N[i,first] where first is a vector that describes the first year for which data are available? I.e, first = c(1985, 2000, 1997, …).
 
After estimating first year abundance N[i,1], the following years are estimated using a loop
for (t in 2:T)
I would then replace this with
for (t in (first+1):T)
or perhaps
for (t in (first+1):last)
where “last” is a vector that describes the last year for which data is availave (e.g. last=c(1995, 2010, 2001, …).
 
Would such a modification of the Dail-Madsen model be ok? Is there some assumption of the Dail-Madsen model that might be violated?
 
Thanks for your help.
Best, Beni

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
parts:
Dear Beni,

I think that you can do two things to alleviate the computational burden of this notorious model in your case:
(1) You can vectorize your analysis, by stringing out all the counts in a single vector, instead of organising them into a regular, 2-dimensional array. The latter means that all the missing responses will be estimated as well in the MCMC updating, adding unnecessarily to the computational burden. For highly imbalanced data sets in hierarchical models such as occupancy and Nmix models etc., this is always one of the first things that one must do to speed up a model.

(2) However, internally, you will then still estimate a lot of latent variables for every site (i) and every year (t). I think that it might be possible to fit a sort of "conditional" DM model, where conditional means "conditional on the years in which you observe data at a site". This would be similar in spirit to the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model, where survival is modelled conditional upon first capture. You could look up BUGS code for the CJS model to see how one may define a vector of first (and in your case, last) observations and then fit the model only to those periods for a site.

I think that such a version of the DM should work, though it would rest upon the untested assumption that the missing value pattern (i.e., whether there is or there is not any count at a site in a year) is ignorable. Comments welcome especially on the 2nd point.

Kind regards  ---  Marc

messages.author: 403be63af7ebf220
messages.subject: Re: Dail-Madsen model with "staggered entry"
parts:
I also replied to this, but forgot to reply to all...


Hi Beni,

I think you could do this, but would need to make sure that you use the correct expected value of abundance for the "first data year". If the first data year is after the first year of the study, then the expected value would depend on the expected value of abundance from the previous year(s). For the "trend" model, which is just a model of geometric growth, you could do something like:

EN[i,1] <- lambda[i] # Expected value of abundance in year 1
for(t in 2:first[i]) {
  EN[i,t] <- EN[i,t-1]*gamma[i] # Expected value of abundance in year 2
  }
for(t in first[i]:T) {
  N[i,t] ~ dpois(EN[i,t])
  }

For this particular model, if gamma is constant over time, you could simply use:

EN[i,t] <- lambda[i]*gamma^first[i]

Note, however, that you should get similar results using either the expected values of N or the latent realized values of N (the approach you are trying to avoid), although the variance of the later will be greater. Also note that this is one of those cases where "gamma" is normally called "lambda" in the ecological literature, making things somewhat confusing.

Hope this helps. Let us know how it turns out.

Richard
